read.title: Why carbon mixes its orbitals
text: A carbon atom has four valence electrons: two in a 2s orbital and two in 2p orbitals. Yet methane has four identical C–H bonds pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron. Valence bond theory explains this with hybridization: the 2s orbital and all three 2p orbitals mix to form four equivalent sp³ hybrid orbitals, about 109.5° apart, each holding one electron for bonding.

When carbon forms a double bond, it mixes the 2s with only two of its p orbitals. The three sp² hybrids lie in a plane at 120°, and the leftover p orbital stands perpendicular to that plane. In ethylene, the sp² orbitals form σ bonds by head-on overlap, while the two leftover p orbitals overlap side by side to make a π bond. Twisting one end would pull the p orbitals apart and break the π bond, so rotation about C=C is restricted.

In a triple bond, carbon is sp: two hybrids point 180° apart, and two p orbitals remain to form two π bonds. Because sp orbitals have more s character, they hold electrons closer to the nucleus. That is why the C–H bond of ethyne is shorter and stronger than the C–H bonds of ethane.
